subtitles.text: Have you ever felt bad without really understanding why?
It’s as if a part of you knows something is wrong, but you just can't put it into words.
Actually, there is a psychological concept that might be eating away at you every day without you knowing it.
And I really don't understand why they didn't teach us this in school.
There was literally a before and after for me when I learned about this concept.
And that concept is cognitive dissonance.
Today, not only will we see why it might be eating away at you right now, but most importantly, we’ll see how to resolve it so we can use it to our advantage.
Cognitive dissonance is a state of tension that occurs when there is a conflict between our values, our thoughts, and our actions.
It comes from a mismatch between the things we believe and the way we act.
Being in dissonance means thinking one thing and acting in another way.
It’s like having one foot on two different boats, and the further apart the boats drift, the more dissonance you feel and the more painful and uncomfortable it becomes.
And the really important thing about dissonance is that this gap creates a sort of pain and psychological tension.
Because when there is an unresolved gap between our thoughts and our actions, we feel anxiety, sadness, and guilt.
One of the most telling examples of cognitive dissonance is a person who smokes while knowing full well that it’s bad for their health.
The action is the act of smoking.
And the belief is that smoking is bad for one's health.
Another example I’ve experienced very often is when you have lots of ambitious plans, but you keep spending your time on video games or scrolling through social media.
When we are in dissonance , we eat ourselves up inside because we know full well we are doing something that isn't necessarily good for us, or we aren't doing something that would have been.
Good for us.
And there are thousands of other possible examples of dissonance, like when our goal is to save money but we give in and buy something super expensive that isn't useful at all.
When you know you need to be productive but spend 3 hours on TikTok, when you’re careful about what you eat and then suddenly go to McDonald’s three times in a row, when you stay.
In a relationship even though you’re not really happy deep down, when you want to lose weight but keep putting off exercising, and so on and so forth.
And what’s interesting about dissonance is that we can try to lie to ourselves as much as we want.
We can try to justify ourselves as much as we want.
Yeah, but I bought it because it was on sale.
Yeah, I have the right to treat myself.
Yeah, cigarettes help me de-stress, it's great.
Yeah, I wasn't productive, but I learned a bunch of cool stuff on TikTok and all that, but deep down, we know we didn't do the right thing.
By the way, a little culture break: this feeling has a name, it's called akrasia.
"Crasia" is the same root found in procrastination.
Akrasia is the act of acting against your own better judgment .
And as long as you're in a state of akrasia, you can try all the therapy in the world.
Practice gratitude, try meditating, do introspection, spend time with friends, travel, or whatever.
As long as there's this gap, as long as there's this dissonance, you won't manage to feel better.
There will always be this little invisible sense of unease inside us.
And if that’s your case, the more you keep putting off what’s important to you, the more stressed, frustrated, and unhappy you’ll feel.
If you feel bad, it’s surely because there are things you know you should do that you aren’t doing.
Because basically, like all the functions of our brain, cognitive dissonance is something that's supposed to be beneficial for us.
It’s a mechanism meant to tell you, "OK, you internally think this thing is bad, you are currently doing this thing that is bad, you need to change that quickly, otherwise I'm going to keep.
Making you feel unhappy."
And technically, there are three main solutions to resolve our dissonance.
The first, and most difficult, is changing our behavior to align it with our beliefs and values.
We know our values are good, but our actions aren't aligned with those values.
So, we will need to change our actions to be able to get as close as possible to our values.
For example, I would like to lose weight because I feel my health is declining, I get out of breath faster and I get sick more often.
Therefore, I value being in good health and being physically fit.
Yet, in my actions, I keep putting off the moment when I will sign up for the gym to go exercise.
So there is a dissonance here, and the best way to bridge this dissonance and stop all the stress and frustration that comes with it is just to take the action aligned with my values.
Which is to go work out .
We know it's the right thing to do, we just have to go and do it.
This solution is clearly the most difficult one.
It's the one we tend to avoid the most and do the least.
But what is certain is that if our values are good, it's the best possible solution to bridge our dissonance.
The second solution we have at our disposal is a little bit simpler, but it is still difficult.
This time, it will be to change our values to bring them closer to our actions.
We must be careful with this solution because if our values are good and it's our actions that are bad, well, if we try to change our values, we will just completely destroy ourselves.
However, this solution applies well.
If our values and beliefs are bad to begin with and our actions are good, then it is coherent to modify our values to bridge the dissonance and keep our good actions.
If we go back to the health and sports example, perhaps you want to exercise more, but you are already doing well, you are already in great health, you already do a lot of sports.
But you've just developed a poor vision, poor beliefs about what a man or woman is supposed to look like.
You've seen super muscular and fit people on social media who only post photos under good lighting, with a pump , who have been doing this for 10 years , who watch their nutrition, and.
Who think about nothing else their whole lives.
And you, are comparing your body to that, and so you just want to do even more sports to bridge your dissonance.
But here, there is a good chance that it is actually your values that are bad and your actions are already good.
So, the parameter to change to reduce your dissonance and feel better is mainly to work on your beliefs to have healthier beliefs about what it means to have a beautiful and healthy body.
So, we have solution number 1, which is to align our actions with our beliefs because our beliefs are good, but our actions are not.
Next , we have solution number 2, which is to align our values with our actions because our actions are already good, but this time it's our values that are not.
And the third solution available to us is the simplest, and it's the one we all tend to gravitate toward.
The third solution is to change nothing about our values or our actions, but to try to escape and mitigate the dissonance.
It's like if two boats were drifting apart and you were in between them, and instead of pulling them together or jumping into one, you just stay right in the middle and take a painkiller.
To stop feeling the pain and physical discomfort.
And to escape the dissonance, we have two main options.
The first one is the use of supernormal stimuli.
I talk about it in detail in this video if you're interested.
Basically, we can call anything a supernormal stimulus if it's a source of intense, immediate dopamine that provides strong short-term pleasure.
Video games, alcohol, drugs, cigarettes , porn, social media, series, junk food , and so on.
Obviously, they aren't all equal at all, but they all share two things in common.
A large dose of immediate pleasure and, most importantly, the escape from our negative emotions.
All supernormal stimuli share the common trait of suppressing our limbic system, which is the part of our brain responsible for managing emotions.
So, when we play video games, use social media, smoke, and so on, we reduce the negative emotions we feel and therefore simultaneously reduce the pain of the dissonance.
We use supernormal stimuli to escape and forget our dissonance.
And that's why human beings spend an average of 5 hours a day on their phones.
It's because we all have points of dissonance in our lives that we are trying to drown out.
And the second possible escape option is through rationalization.
To rationalize is to try to convince yourself through reason that your beliefs and your actions aren't, in fact, that misaligned.
We will try to mitigate it by finding arguments and adding new parameters.
We will try to add other factors into the equation.
We will try to find excuses and use others to try to justify ourselves.
So rationalization is also an escape from the problem, and it's once again trying to forget and mitigate the dissonance rather than resolve it.
Is, of course, a bad solution, and despite all the harm it does, research continues to show that it is the solution we tend to repeat in a loop as humans to mitigate our dissonance.
We all find ourselves excuses on a loop every day rather than trying to change our actions.
Because finding excuses and not questioning ourselves will inevitably be much simpler and much faster.
To give you a few examples, rationalizing is smoking while knowing it's bad for us and telling ourselves, "Yes, but hey, everyone around me smokes too, so it's not a big deal."
Yes, but my grandfather smoked and he lived to be 90.
Yes, but hey, I exercise a lot, so it's fine, it balances out.
Or it's when you steal something from the supermarket and you say, "Yes, but hey, I think the biggest thieves between the two of us are actually the big retailers.""Yes, but hey, everyone would have.
Done that.""Yes, but hey, I needed it and I didn't hurt anyone."
Or it's when you keep putting off your exercise and diet and you say, "Yes, but hey, these last 6 months, I really haven't had much time for myself.""Yes, but hey, it wasn't really the.
Right time."
Yes, but hey, I'm just not cut out for sports.
Yeah, but I'm too much of a foodie, too.
All these are justifications that aim to mitigate our own dissonance.
It's when we know deep down that what we are doing is bad but we find excuses for ourselves so we don't feel too bad about it.
And there is a quote by Mark Manson that I really like.
Smart people procrastinate more because they are so smart that they manage to find twice as many excuses not to do something.
That sentence is excellent.
You might think that the smarter you are, the less dissonance you would have, but actually, it's the opposite.
The more intelligent we are, the more we succeed in bullshitting ourselves and finding excuses to justify our own dissonance.
We become so skilled at debating that we turn into experts at arguing against ourselves.
And by the way, if you have any doubt and aren't really sure if you're in dissonance, the fact that you're justifying yourself is already proof number one that you are.
There is a phrase that is hard to hear but very interesting.
Someone who is not in dissonance does not seek to justify themselves.
Someone who is comfortable with buying things won't tell themselves, "Yes, but I had to buy it because it was on sale; anyway, I got a good deal.""Yes, but I have the right to treat.
Myself once in a while."
Or someone who is comfortable with their body doesn't spend their time justifying why they didn't have time to work out and why exercise isn't for them, and all that.
We don't need excuses when we know we are doing the right thing.
If you keep finding excuses for doing something or stopping something, that thing is probably what you should focus on that would bring you the most peace.
The thing we try so hard to defend with our excuses is surely the first thing we should focus on because the void you feel is just the space left by what you refuse to.
Do .
You can either endure the pain of dissonance or the pain of change.
And the pain of dissonance is much worse, much more stressful, and will continue to eat away at you slowly.
All this research on cognitive dissonance made me realize something that completely transformed my view on the subject.
Dissonance is one of the greatest forms of discomfort, stress, and unease.
Everything can be going wonderfully in our life.
As long as we have one area that is in dissonance, we will feel sad and empty and won't understand why.
Even with the best lifestyle, if there is dissonance regarding a relationship, a bad habit, or something we know we should do, well, we will continue to suffer little by little.
So the main lesson to take away from all this is that we must become true hunters of dissonance.
We must go to war against dissonance.
And our best weapon for that is integrity.
Because integrity is the opposite of dissonance.
Integrity is the alignment between your values, your words, and your actions.
Being a person of integrity means bringing those two boats closer together and bridging the gap between what you think and how you act.
Integrity is by far the best solution to improve your self-esteem, be more in tune with your emotions, and above all, unlock an infallible peace within yourself.
Because resolving your dissonance is essential to making your life much more peaceful.
And it's a level of peace that very few people will experience because, as we've seen, most people seek to flee from it and numb it.
And you and I, unfortunately, are no exception to this rule because it’s much easier to run from it than to resolve it.
Especially these days with all the super-stimuli we have at our disposal.
But the first step to overcoming this trap is to become an expert detector of your own excuses.
We must learn to observe our own signs of fleeing from dissonance.
We must observe when we try to overstimulate ourselves, rationalize, or find excuses , because that points directly to where the dissonance lies.
So, the right exercise for this is to ask yourself: in what area of my life are my actions not aligned with my beliefs and my values?
How does this affect me?
How do I feel when that happens?
What technique am I using to try to numb my dissonance?
Am I overstimulating myself ?
Am I making excuses for myself?
If so , which ones?
For example, I’ve been playing video games a bit too much lately and it wasn't at all aligned with my values and goals, but I couldn't help myself.
And look at how I try to numb the dissonance.
There, I already have a first excuse: "I couldn't help myself."
So, I did the exercise of writing down all the justifications I told myself to try to open the games instead of working.
And it's incredible how good we are at bullshitting ourselves.
I’d tell myself, I worked hard, I deserve to play a little bit.
I’ll just play for 5 minutes; it’s like taking a little break.
I have the right to do things I enjoy, otherwise my daily life would suck.
I just want to check something in the game.
I just want to test something out.
Just 2 minutes, I can handle it.
Come on, please.
I have the right to treat myself.
What’s the point of only working if I can’t have any fun?
My friends play video games too.
I’ve worked really hard these past six months.
Come on, playing a little bit has never killed anyone.
It’s impressive how many justifications we can come up with and swallow to explain away our discomfort, which is itself tied to our dissonance.
And by the way, a small but important clarification: some of these justifications might actually be completely true.
Many of our excuses are perfectly valid.
The goal isn't to ignore everything and become an excuse-smashing machine.
The goal is to manage to spot them all and then be able to make our own decisions as free men or women.
The goal isn't to shut down all our excuses by closing our eyes and going into "work work , discipline mode.
The goal is to see that we are justifying ourselves, to try to see what dissonance we are justifying, and then to make a decision about it.
Maybe I really have worked hard these last six months and allowing myself to play a little bit of video games isn't unreasonable.
And so, the act of playing video games isn't inherently bad.
It’s more the belief that I must only work that is wrong and needs to change.
But on the other hand, if I’ve spent the last ten days playing video games while completely slacking off on my work, it's the opposite; the excuses I'm making are just to keep playing video.
Games and staying in my comfort zone instead of doing the harder work.
So it’s a very subtle battle, and that’s where integrity comes into play.
Integrity is your greatest weapon in your hunt for dissonance.
You must have the courage to lie to yourself as little as possible.
You need to clarify the equation as much as possible, become aware of your values, your actions, and your excuses, and have the courage to make the right decision in the face of it all.
You can then choose whether to change your beliefs or change your behavior to have more integrity in your life.
Because as long as you let dissonance reign, you will be condemned to stress, frustration, and unhappiness .
No one is perfect.
Everyone experiences dissonance.
We fail and we start over again and again.
I make personal development videos, and I’ve given in to video games a bit too much.
We all have dissonances, but what matters is what we do with them, and especially how long it takes us to act.
Integrity is the greatest form of self-love you can give yourself and the courage to follow the flame burning inside you.
Act in accordance with your ambitions.
Do what is right, not what is easy.
